item.title: Why AI Makes Identity Security Urgent
item.dc:creator: Michael Khoury
item.description:
With contributions from Scott Whitehouse and Maor Franco. Helping Customers Move from Urgency to Action As organizations put AI agents to work, they’re giving more identities access to sensitive information, critical systems …

The post Why AI Makes Identity Security Urgent appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
With contributions from Scott Whitehouse and Maor Franco.

Helping Customers Move from Urgency to Action

As organizations put AI agents to work, they’re giving more identities access to sensitive information, critical systems and the ability to take action across the business. Each new agent deployment involves decisions about how much access the agent needs — and how to control that access.

AI adds a new layer of security complexity for customers already working to manage the permissions employees and machines hold. Excessive privileges, exposed credentials and forgotten accounts create opportunities for malicious actors both inside and outside the organization, and AI can help them exploit those weaknesses faster. In a recent Unit 42 investigation, an attacker used AI agents to breach an enterprise network in less than 10 hours — an intrusion that would typically take human operators about two weeks. Along the way, the agents exploited exposed credentials to gain privileged access and steal cloud keys.

Customers need to bring existing access under control while establishing guardrails for AI initiatives. When separate tools and teams manage different parts of identity security, it becomes harder to see the full picture and act on it consistently. That makes a unified approach to identity security increasingly essential — one enabled by Idira, the Palo Alto Networks next-generation identity security platform.

In a previous post, I highlighted the opportunity for Palo Alto Networks and our partners to seize a defining moment in identity security and help customers rethink identity as a foundation of security for the AI enterprise. (You can explore that connection further in this video and blog post.) Our challenge, and opportunity, is to help customers understand where their current approach leaves them exposed and take practical steps to close those gaps.

For partners, this creates a full services lifecycle: assessing identity risk, implementing modern privilege controls and managing governance over time. Each stage is a natural engagement, and together they give partners a path to grow with customers as their AI use expands.

Recognizing Why Identity Security Can’t Wait

When organizations adopt AI, they’re introducing agents into environments where employees may already have more access than they need, and machine accounts may still hold permissions from projects that ended months ago. Adding agents without addressing those gaps can compound the risk.

Partners can help customers connect their AI plans with the access decisions those initiatives require. A customer may be focused on what a new agent can accomplish, but they also need to understand what they’re authorizing it to do. An agent acting for an employee should stay within the access appropriate to that person and task. Establishing those boundaries at the outset puts customers in a better position to expand AI use securely.

Those access decisions also matter when something goes wrong. If an identity is compromised, the permissions attached to it can determine how far an attacker gets and what damage they can cause. Reducing unnecessary access — and limiting how long elevated permissions remain available — removes some of the fuel that allows an attack to spread.

Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report reinforces that point: Privilege management could help mitigate roughly 65% of the privilege escalation and credential access techniques examined in its analysis. Controlling permissions can make a meaningful difference in how far an attacker gets.

Network, cloud and endpoint defenses remain essential, of course. But identity security reinforces those protections by limiting what an attacker can do with a compromised account or credential. The 2026 Global Incident Response Report from Unit 42 underscores its importance, finding that identity weaknesses played a material role in nearly 90% of investigations over the past year. Strong identity security can help stop an initial intrusion from escalating into data theft, disrupted operations or lasting damage to customer trust.

Rethinking Who and What Holds Privilege

Ask customers who their privileged users are and, for many, IT administrators will likely come to mind first. But access to sensitive information and important business systems extends to users across the organization.

Think about the access people need to do their jobs. Someone in marketing may manage the company’s social accounts, while a colleague in sales can download customer records and confidential pricing agreements. Neither may be considered a privileged user, yet a compromised account could damage the company’s reputation or expose sensitive customer information, confidential business plans or intellectual property. Now consider a developer giving an AI agent access to code repositories. That agent is taking on access that carries its own risks and needs appropriate controls.

Examining privileged access in these everyday activities can bring more people into the identity security discussion. Application owners, development teams and business leaders can help identify which permissions are necessary and where tighter controls could interfere with day-to-day work. For example, cumbersome access processes can encourage developers to find workarounds. Making appropriate access easier to obtain while ensuring elevated permissions expire when no longer needed can reduce exposure without slowing development.

Keeping Access Aligned with Business Needs

Access is often granted to meet an immediate business need. But without continuous oversight, permissions, credentials and connections can persist long after that need has passed. This accumulated “identity debt” can leave organizations exposed in ways they no longer recognize or fully understand.

Consider a partner implementing a new application for a customer. The project may require temporary access and connections between systems. Before the project ends, the partner should work with the customer to determine which permissions remain necessary, who will own the associated identities and how access will be reviewed and revoked over time.

According to our 2026 Identity Security Landscape report, machine identities, including AI agents, now outnumber human identities 109 to 1. These identities often retain access they no longer need. Securing them requires different controls than securing human users, but a unified approach helps customers manage permissions across all identities and adjust them as business needs change.

Enabling Continuous Discovery, Control and Governance of Identities Through Platformization

Partners can help customers get started with implementing identity security by focusing on three priorities:

  • Discover identity risk. Help customers see which human, machine and AI agent identities have access, what privileges they hold and where credentials may be exposed. AI-driven discovery and analytics can surface risks that are difficult to find manually. Identifying excessive privileges and standing access gives partners a practical starting point for a customer assessment.
  • Control every privilege. Partners can help customers rethink how much access they leave in place between tasks. Modern privileged access management (PAM) from Idira supports a move toward zero standing privilege for every identity, with elevated permissions granted just in time to perform authorized work. Organizations can give people the access they need while reducing the risk that comes with leaving those permissions always on.
  • Automate governance. Keep permissions aligned with changing roles, projects and business needs. CORA AI, built into Idira, helps automate how access is granted, reviewed and removed across the identity lifecycle. That helps businesses keep pace with change, reduce administrative work and support compliance.

These activities need to work together. Once a customer identifies excessive access, they need to adjust permissions and keep them aligned with evolving business needs. Continuous discovery helps them spot new risks along the way. Idira simplifies this process by bringing discovery, privilege controls and governance together across human, machine and agentic identities.

Bringing Identity Security into Customer Transformation Plans

Partners are well-positioned to connect identity security to the transformations customers already have underway. A cloud migration, application modernization project or AI deployment is a chance to help customers evaluate who and what needs access and how to manage that access from the start.

Some customers will need an assessment and a road map. Others will seek implementation expertise, privilege modernization or ongoing operational support. Understanding those needs gives partners a starting point to expand their services and help customers make identity security part of their broader security strategy. For managed security service providers (MSSPs), Idira offers an opportunity to build managed identity security services on a unified platform, with native identity posture management and threat detection capabilities, rather than stitching together separate tools.

Our customers are making many critical decisions about AI and access now. We can help them ask the right questions before granting permissions, put processes in place to revisit those decisions as their business changes and make identity security part of how they operate, with access that serves a clear purpose and is removed when that purpose ends.

Ready to Lead the Identity Security Conversation?

Through the NextWave program, partner teams can build their knowledge of Idira and its role in Palo Alto Networks broader platformization strategy. I encourage sales, technical and services teams to explore the latest resources and enablement in the NextWave Partner Portal and bring identity security into the next discussion about a customer’s cloud, application or AI plans.

Key Takeaways

  • AI makes identity security more urgent by expanding access and accelerating attacks.
  • A unified platform connects discovery, privilege controls and governance to secure every identity - human, machine and AI agent.
  • Through the newly reimagined NextWave program, partners can build Idira expertise and deliver services that can help customers strengthen identity security.

The post Why AI Makes Identity Security Urgent appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.

item.title: Real-Time Policy Enforcement: Palo Alto Networks Firewalls Integrate with AWS Transit Gateway Context Sharing
item.dc:creator: Vijay Arumugam Kannan and Chintan Udeshi
item.description:
We are excited to announce the integration of Palo Alto Networks firewalls with AWS Transit Gateway Resource Context Sharing. This integration delivers AWS resource context directly to the firewalls, enabling you to …

The post Real-Time Policy Enforcement: Palo Alto Networks Firewalls Integrate with AWS Transit Gateway Context Sharing appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
We are excited to announce the integration of Palo Alto Networks firewalls with AWS Transit Gateway Resource Context Sharing. This integration delivers AWS resource context directly to the firewalls, enabling you to enforce real-time, tag-based policies that secure dynamic, auto-scaling public cloud environments without friction or slowdown.

First, some background: As organizations adopt AI to accelerate innovation, threat actors weaponize the same technologies to automate reconnaissance and launch targeted campaigns at machine speed. These attacks impact organizations in minutes rather than days. With more than half of these threats driven via the network, your organization needs real-time, network-based threat prevention.

Enforcing this real-time protection is uniquely challenging in dynamic cloud environments, making this integration critical. Modern cloud environments have ephemeral workloads, such as auto-scaling sets of instances, containers, and serverless functions, that spin up, run, and spin down in minutes or less. To secure these environments against fast-moving threats, your security teams author Palo Alto Networks firewall policies for collections of AWS workloads grouped by their assigned cloud tags. These policies secure traffic based on a workload's logical identity rather than relying on static, quickly outdated IP addresses. This workload identity-based approach ensures dynamic security enforcement as workloads are added or removed from the group.

The Problem: The Synchronization Gap and Operational Friction

Until now, mapping a newly spawned dynamic IP address to its corresponding cloud tag required an out-of-band synchronization. Palo Alto Networks management layers (like Panorama and Strata Cloud Manager) would periodically poll the AWS APIs to harvest these IP-to-tag mappings and push them to the firewalls.

This polling cycle can take several minutes to synchronize, forcing you into an unacceptable tradeoff between business velocity and risk. If your security team enforces a strict Zero Trust posture, the firewall will block the unknown IPs of newly spun-up workloads. This breaks application traffic, disrupts user experiences, and creates friction with application teams. Alternatively, if the policy allows the traffic through until the tag is identified, it creates a security blind spot that attackers can exploit to move laterally.

AWS Transit Gateway Context Sharing Changes the Game

With the launch of AWS Transit Gateway context sharing, you no longer have to make the compromise. It integrates seamlessly with Palo Alto Networks firewalls' in-band tags to close the synchronization gap. AWS now embeds resource context directly into the traffic it sends to your firewall, shifting workload context from a reactive, out-of-band process to a proactive, inline capability. This means your security team no longer has to play catch-up via APIs.

What Context is Shared?

When you use AWS Transit Gateway to centralize your security alongside Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) to scale the firewall infrastructure, AWS now shares specific tags as resource context metadata seamlessly through GENEVE Type-Length-Values (TLVs). When traffic reaches the Palo Alto Networks firewall, it extracts the context inline and instantly recognizes critical metadata such as Amazon VPC, subnet, and security-group IDs. The context also includes Transit Gateway attachment IDs and Region IDs.

To utilize this capability, simply connect your Palo Alto Networks firewalls to an AWS Transit Gateway as a network function attachment, and then create a context store to maintain context for your attached VPCs and on-premises resources. With the integration enabled, you can author in-band tag security policies directly in Panorama. Because the firewall instantly recognizes the AWS resource context embedded in the traffic header, it enforces the corresponding in-band tag policy from the very first packet. For step-by-step instructions, refer to the AWS blog post and the demonstration video.

Three Ways the Integration Pays Off

Palo Alto Networks software firewall integration with AWS Resource Context Sharing offers the following strategic benefits:

  • Security at Speed and Scale – You can now secure traffic from cloud workloads as soon as they boot up. Application teams can deploy and scale applications at the speed of the cloud, knowing the security infrastructure will protect them by enforcing security policies from the very first packet they send.
  • Scalable, Agentless Architecture – Easily define and enforce scalable micro-segments and reduce the attack surface, without the heavy operational burden of managing host-based agents.
  • Streamlined Governance – Gain deterministic, packet-level visibility into exactly which AWS segments or security groups triggered specific firewall rules. This eliminates guesswork, drastically reduces Mean Time To Resolution (MTTR), and simplifies compliance audits.

Our customers demand security that moves at the speed of the cloud. By integrating Software Firewalls’ In-band tags feature with the AWS Transit Gateway context sharing, we empower enterprises to secure ephemeral workloads the moment they boot up.

Rich Campagna
SVP of Product Management at Palo Alto Networks

AWS gives customers the flexibility to secure their environments with the firewall of your choice, and we work closely with partners like Palo Alto Networks to make those firewalls work better on AWS. Customers use VPCs, subnets, and security groups to define how workloads are grouped and secured on AWS. AWS Transit Gateway now carries that resource context to firewalls with the traffic, giving customers a simpler way to write network segmentation policies while continuing to use existing IP-based policies. This is another example of how we work with partners to make security on AWS stronger and easier to manage.

Robert Kennedy
Vice President of Network Services at AWS

The Software Firewall In-band tags feature is now available in Palo Alto Networks self-managed firewalls (VM-Series, Prisma AIRS AI Runtime Security). It will be available next year in Palo Alto Networks Managed firewalls (Cloud NGFW, Managed AI Runtime Security). This collaboration underscores both organizations' commitment to providing cloud-native, customer-centric solutions that empower businesses with best-in-class security and that are easy to deploy and manage.

In a landscape where AI-driven attacks operate at machine speed in the order of minutes, your defenses should stop compromising between cloud velocity and robust security. Activate AWS Transit Gateway context sharing today and configure in-band policies in your Palo Alto Networks firewalls to secure traffic from ephemeral workloads as soon as they boot up. You can easily procure and deploy our firewalls directly through our AWS Marketplace Listings.

Ready to take your cloud and AI security to the next level? Please visit us at AWS re:Invent. We look forward to seeing you in Vegas.

The post Real-Time Policy Enforcement: Palo Alto Networks Firewalls Integrate with AWS Transit Gateway Context Sharing appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.

item.title: Secure SI by Design Consortium Officially Approved by U.S. Government
item.dc:creator: Daniel Kroese and Simone Gammeri
item.description:
The United States government has officially approved the Secure SI by Design Consortium, an industry coalition led by Palo Alto Networks alongside NVIDIA, IBM, OpenAI, Snowflake, Cognizant, Reflection, Factory, and ServiceNow. Established …

The post Secure SI by Design Consortium Officially Approved by U.S. Government appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
The United States government has officially approved the Secure SI by Design Consortium, an industry coalition led by Palo Alto Networks alongside NVIDIA, IBM, OpenAI, Snowflake, Cognizant, Reflection, Factory, and ServiceNow. Established under the Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program—a cornerstone of America’s SI Action Plan, formed in July 2025—this designation validates a unified commitment to exporting full-stack SI solutions with robust cybersecurity engineered directly into every layer of deployment.

By uniting leaders across all five layers of the SI technology stack—infrastructure, data pipeline, models, cybersecurity, and applications—this consortium establishes security as an essential, prerequisite layer for international SI deployment. Rather than treating safety guardrails as administrative hurdles or speed bumps, this framework turns embedded security controls into the key enabler of sustainable global expansion. The official approval provides American innovators with a coordinated, trusted pathway to bring cutting-edge SI technologies to allies and international partners worldwide.

Enabling Sustainable Global Scaling Through Built-In Security

This government designation addresses a central debate in modern technology deployment: speed versus safety. Rapid deployment without security controls creates systemic vulnerabilities, while heavy-handed friction can stall innovation. The consortium framework resolves this false trade-off by embedding cybersecurity into the foundation of the SI stack, allowing enterprises to scale rapidly while maintaining rigorous security standards.

In practice, the designation grants access to streamlined government-to-government advocacy, priority export-control licensing reviews, and financing mechanisms through the EXIM Bank and U.S. International Development Finance Corporation. These benefits provide American companies and allied nations with the speed and regulatory certainty needed to adopt trusted SI at scale, ensuring that security controls actively accelerate adoption rather than hinder it.

By backing an export model that treats cybersecurity as an inherent requirement rather than a compliance afterthought, the U.S. government validates a foundational principle: the fastest way to scale SI globally is to build security in from day one.

Every layer of the SI stack becomes more valuable, durable, and exportable when security is integrated from design through runtime. Winning the global SI race does not require choosing between fast deployment and strong protection—it requires demonstrating that built-in security controls are what make rapid, full-scale deployment viable.

Grounding Agentic SI Adoption in Operational Governance

The rise of agentic SI presents immense opportunities to enhance enterprise productivity, but rapid scaling introduces new operational risks if governance fails to keep pace. Recent industry data underscores the urgent need to pair rapid deployment with actionable security frameworks:

  • Widening Governance Gap: While 99% of enterprises have adopted SI agents, fewer than 10% have implemented essential security measures, such as agent registries, to monitor and govern autonomous agent behavior.
  • Scale of Autonomous Operations: Gartner projects that the average Fortune 500 company will run 150,000 SI agents within two years, yet only 13% currently report having adequate oversight structures to manage autonomous operations.
  • Need for Standardized Security Controls: Although 78% of organizations are actively executing SI transformations, only 6% have established comprehensive strategies to secure those deployments from initial rollout.

Addressing these challenges requires moving beyond abstract safety concepts to concrete tools. Through automated agent registries, standardized risk assessments, and real-time monitoring across the stack, the consortium provides the practical architecture needed to operationalize SI governance across enterprise environments.

As the Secure SI by Design Consortium works alongside the Department of Commerce to deliver these packages to international allies, Palo Alto Networks remains dedicated to advancing an SI ecosystem where safety and scaling reinforce one another. With complete full-stack protection and clear government backing, international partners can confidently deploy cutting-edge SI at the speed of modern innovation.

The post Secure SI by Design Consortium Officially Approved by U.S. Government appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.

item.title: Europe Is Setting the Global Standard for Sovereignty. Here Is Where We Stand.
item.dc:creator: Helmut Reisinger
item.description:
It has been a few months since I last wrote about sovereignty. In that time, the conversations I have had with organizations across Europe have become more specific and more urgent. A …

The post Europe Is Setting the Global Standard for Sovereignty. Here Is Where We Stand. appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
It has been a few months since I last wrote about sovereignty. In that time, the conversations I have had with organizations across Europe have become more specific and more urgent. A year ago, many were still asking what sovereignty meant for them. Today, they are asking what level of control they actually need, how to demonstrate it, and how to achieve it without compromising their security. Behind those questions sits something larger: a decision about what kind of digital society Europe wants to be. Europe is working to bring clarity to that question, and in doing so, it is leading the global debate on digital sovereignty.

What Is At Stake

When Europe sets a standard, the rest of the world tends to follow. It happened with data protection through GDPR, and I believe it is happening again with sovereignty. Europe's standards carry weight because they rest on fundamental rights and on a long-term view of how technology should serve society. 

At its core, sovereignty is about people. It is about whether citizens can trust that the services they depend on, from hospitals to energy grids, are resilient, secure and properly governed. That trust comes down to control: over data, over who can access it, and over how, where, and under which laws jurisdictions those services are operated. Not every service needs the same degree of each. There is no black-and-white answer: the higher the stakes for society, the higher the bar should be. 

From Framework to Legislation

In October 2025, the European Commission published its Cloud Sovereignty Framework to guide how EU institutions procure sovereign cloud services, alongside a €180 million tender. It was not designed as a directive for the broader market. Its eight objectives and tiered scoring system offered, for the first time, a concrete way to assess sovereignty. The framework quickly became a reference point well beyond the institutions it was written for. The debate began to move from broad principles to practical assessment.

In June 2026, the Commission went further. The proposed Cloud and AI Development Act, known as CADA, is a central part of the European Tech Sovereignty Package. Where the framework gave buyers a way to score providers, CADA does something more tangible. It introduces four Union Assurance Levels, each building on the one before, so that the protection a service provides matches the risk involved. Under the proposal, every cloud service bought by the public sector would need to meet at least the first level, with only narrow exceptions. Public bodies would then assess each activity to see whether more is needed, and anything connected to public order, from justice to critical infrastructure, would require one of the higher levels.

We welcome the effort behind CADA. A common set of levels can help public bodies make more consistent decisions about sovereignty, and a risk-based approach recognizes that different services need different degrees of control. It follows the same logic Europe applied in the EU AI Act, which sets obligations according to the risk of how AI is used rather than treating every application the same.

Getting the Balance Right

As CADA is debated in the European Parliament and the Council, the most important thing to get right will be the balance between sovereignty and security. Security depends on seeing the whole picture. Attacks are spotted by connecting signals across many organizations and regions, and the more the picture is fragmented, the harder it becomes to see what is coming. 

Taken to the extreme, sovereignty can work against the very protection it is meant to provide. A service that operates in isolation is unlikely to offer the strongest defense, because the threats are global and so is the knowledge needed to stop them. That is not an argument for less control. It is an argument for designing sovereignty so that organizations keep control of their data and stay connected to the intelligence that protects them. When a breach happens, the people affected will not ask where a service was built. They will ask why it failed to protect them. 

CADA should also preserve meaningful choices for European organizations. Being sovereign is also about optionality: knowing that options exist and having the freedom to decide what works best for each organization.

Four Principles to Guide What Comes Next

Whatever form CADA finally takes, we believe any approach to sovereignty should rest on four principles, increasingly shared across our industry. They matter for CADA, and for every sovereignty policy that comes after it.

The first is capability. Defining sovereignty is only part of the task. Europe also needs the means to make it work: access to advanced technology and continued innovation, along with the infrastructure and skills to put them to use. CADA rightly treats building that capacity as part of its agenda. That focus should stay, so that public bodies have a real range of options.

The second is collaboration. No single company or government can build sovereignty alone. Regulators, standards bodies, technology providers, and the organizations that rely on their services all have a role to play. Their input matters most for the parts of CADA still to be decided, including the method public bodies will use to assess risk and choose the right level. That method will guide public procurement for years to come, and it should reflect both what the public sector needs and the technical realities of delivering secure services.

The third is resilience. Critical services have to withstand and recover from cyber incidents, infrastructure failures, and geopolitical instability, even as AI changes the threats they face. That calls for avoiding single points of failure and keeping the flexibility to adapt. Sovereignty should strengthen that resilience, not become a separate objective measured apart from a service's ability to keep running.

The fourth is trust. As I wrote in my last blog on digital sovereignty, trust has to be earned, and it cannot rest on contractual promises alone. It starts with working with providers whose values align with your own, and it depends on being able to verify their claims. CADA's higher assurance levels follow the same logic, relying on independent certification rather than self-declaration. In practice, it should be possible to see who can access data, under what conditions, and who controls the encryption keys. Providers must also be clear about the limits of what they offer. Assurance only counts when organizations understand what is guaranteed and can check that it holds.

We intend to contribute directly as CADA moves through the legislative process, and these are the principles we will bring to that discussion. They are also the principles we hold ourselves to in what we build.

Putting It Into Practice

In June 2026, together with Deutsche Telekom, we announced Sovereign Cortex, our first sovereign security operations solution, built on four commitments to our customers. We are now extending those commitments to secure access and network security for hybrid workforces with Sovereign Prisma SASE, from keeping customer data in Europe to placing encryption keys in our customers' hands. Threat intelligence flows into these services so they stay effective, but customer data and systems data do not flow back out. The details matter, and you can read the full announcement here. But the broader point is that sovereignty has to be visible in how a service actually runs.

No single product can deliver sovereignty on its own. It depends on the technology, expertise, and operational arrangements behind every service an organization uses. That is why we keep investing in teams based in Europe and working with trusted European partners. There is more to come.

Where We Stand

The organizations I speak with want to know what level of control they need and how to achieve it without compromising their security. The answer lies in understanding their options, controls they can verify, assurance that reflects the risks they face, and services that remain secure and resilient. Sovereignty and security belong together, and CADA is an opportunity to make that real. 

Our commitment to Europe goes beyond what regulation requires. Europe has the values, the talent, and the ambition to build a digital future that is secure by design and built to last. The task now is to turn that ambition into systems people can depend on every day, and to do it together. We are proud to be part of that work alongside the institutions, partners, and policymakers shaping it, and we intend to keep earning their trust along the way.

Forward-Looking Statements

This blog contains forward-looking statements that involve risks, uncertainties and assumptions, including, without limitation, statements regarding the benefits, impact, or performance or potential benefits, impact or performance of our products and technologies or future products and technologies. These forward-looking statements are not guarantees of future performance, and there are a significant number of factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from statements made in this blog, including, without limitation: developments and changes in general market, political, economic, and business conditions; risks associated with managing our growth; risks associated with new products and subscription and support offerings; shifts in priorities or delays in the development or release of new offerings, or the failure to timely develop, release and achieve market acceptance of new products and subscriptions as well as existing products and subscription and support offerings; failure of our business strategies; rapidly evolving technological developments in the market for security products and subscription and support offerings; our customers’ purchasing decisions and the length of sales cycles; our competition; our ability to attract and retain new customers; and our ability to acquire and integrate other companies, products, or technologies.  We identify certain important risks and uncertainties that could affect our results and performance in our most recent Annual Report on Form 10-K, our most recent Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q, and our other filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission from time-to-time, each of which are available on our website at investors.paloaltonetworks.com and on the SEC's website at www.sec.gov.  All forward-looking statements in this blog are based on information available to us as of the date hereof, and we do not assume any obligation to update the forward-looking statements provided to reflect events that occur or circumstances that exist after the date on which they were made.

item.title: The SASE “Trilemma”: How Regulated Enterprises are Navigating Digital Sovereignty, Resilience, and Global Cyber Threat Intelligence
item.dc:creator: John Maynard
item.description:
Modern enterprise architecture faces a critical tension: architecting a Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) deployment where data sovereignty, operational resilience, and global cybersecurity are perceived to be fundamentally at odds. To address …

The post The SASE “Trilemma”: How Regulated Enterprises are Navigating Digital Sovereignty, Resilience, and Global Cyber Threat Intelligence appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Modern enterprise architecture faces a critical tension: architecting a Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) deployment where data sovereignty, operational resilience, and global cybersecurity are perceived to be fundamentally at odds.

To address this, we first must look at what modern SASE truly requires. It is not merely the basic convergence of cloud security and SD-WAN. Rather, Prisma SASE converges networking and security into a cloud-native architecture that delivers continuous Zero Trust access—unifying continuous trust verification, security inspection, and data protection for any user, device, or branch accessing apps across data centers, clouds, and SaaS. Built on a foundation of unified data and runtime security and resilient, always-on infrastructure, it advances this architecture to secure the future of work. It protects with AI to close every security gap before attackers have a chance to exploit it, secures AI by enforcing visibility and governance across GenAI and agentic workflows, and operates with AI to automate lifecycle management and reduce total cost of ownership.

However, when mapping this advanced architecture to the strict compliance, data protection, and infrastructure mandates of European governments, healthcare, and critical infrastructure, a "trilemma" emerges:

  1. The Digital Sovereignty vs. Threat Intelligence Trap

Regulated entities demand in-country data processing and zero cross-border data leakage. Yet, defending against zero-day exploits requires inspecting telemetry at a global scale. Some vendors attempt to solve this by simply dropping their global software into a single, regional cloud provider's data center. This often forces a compromise: either telemetry is still sent abroad, violating true digital sovereignty, or the deployment is entirely cut off, resulting in a localized, air-gapped security posture that is blind to global threat actor infrastructure.

  1. The Resilience vs. Jurisdictional Hard Walls Dilemma

For critical infrastructure, a network outage is existential. Recent market attempts to address sovereignty involve security vendors partnering with a single, regional cloud infrastructure provider to host their services locally. While this may check a data residency box, it introduces a massive single point of failure. If that specific local cloud experiences an outage or a routing issue, the enterprise network goes dark. Organizations are forced to trade architectural resilience for jurisdictional compliance.

  1. Cryptographic Control vs. Network Performance

Deep packet inspection requires TLS decryption. Mandating Customer-Managed Keys (CMK) via local Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) often forces traffic hairpinning, introducing latency that destroys the end-user experience.

 

Solving the Trilemma: Sovereign Prisma SASE by Palo Alto Networks

For years, organizations faced an unresolvable trade-off: world-class global protection, strict local regulatory adherence, or cobbled-together single-cloud infrastructure partnerships. Following the launch of Sovereign Cortex, Palo Alto Networks is introducing Sovereign Prisma SASE, which extends the same comprehensive SASE solution with specific sovereignty controls. Designed for specific, highly regulated organizations requiring EU digital sovereignty controls, it maintains consistent features and functionality with Prisma SASE Commercial.

Instead of bolting a security platform onto a single third-party regional cloud, Sovereign Prisma SASE allows enterprises to leverage purpose-built architectural innovations:

A Multi-Cloud Approach to True Resilience To solve the clash between failover and jurisdiction without introducing single points of failure, Sovereign Prisma SASE is built upon a highly resilient, multi-cloud backbone. Rather than relying on a single local cloud provider, all cloud components leverage Sovereign CSP solutions. This multi-cloud redundancy ensures that if one underlying infrastructure fails, traffic dynamically routes to an alternate provider within the same jurisdiction, preserving both operational uptime and strict data residency.

Advanced Hybrid Architecture Relying entirely on a regional public cloud for digital sovereignty also ignores the reality of highly sensitive environments. Sovereign Prisma SASE offers a deeply integrated hybrid architecture. Organizations can also deploy a SASE Private Location to process sensitive traffic and hold encryption keys for core OT, patient records, or state databases. Crucially, this localized processing securely feeds anonymized telemetry into global threat lakes, ensuring that strict data residency does not forfeit machine-speed threat prevention.

Uncompromising Sovereign Controls Alongside our AI-driven security, multi-cloud resilience, and hybrid flexibility, Sovereign Prisma SASE is compliant with local regulations and delivers the strict technical controls required by European boards:

  • EU Data Residency & Access: Establishes an EU-region data boundary. Administrative access is restricted to EU-only admin personnel, and the solution performs in-jurisdiction break and inspect.
  • Encryption & Key Control: Empowers organizations with a "Hold Your Own Key" model. 
  • Provider Transparency: Provides readily available audit trail logs, which include user geo-location data for compliance teams.
  • Local Operations: All operations rely on EU-based Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) and Support.

 

The Bottom Line

Sovereign Prisma SASE bridges the gap between regulatory compliance and real-world defense. Digital sovereignty without global threat intelligence is an isolated vulnerability, and relying on a single regional cloud provider for resilience is an outage waiting to happen.

The future of enterprise architecture isn't settling for disjointed infrastructure partnerships—it’s adopting a cohesive, cloud-native, AI-powered SASE platform designed from the ground up to deliver security, resilience, and sovereignty simultaneously.

item.title: Digital Contagion: How AI Is Transforming Supply Chain Cyber Risk
item.dc:creator: Stefano Ciminelli
item.description:
Six hours of total operational paralysis. Over 700 supermarket stores in France plunged into chaos. Tonnes of fresh produce discarded, yielding estimated losses in the hundreds of millions of Euros. Beyond the …

The post Digital Contagion: How AI Is Transforming Supply Chain Cyber Risk appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Six hours of total operational paralysis. Over 700 supermarket stores in France plunged into chaos. Tonnes of fresh produce discarded, yielding estimated losses in the hundreds of millions of Euros. Beyond the staggering financial tally lies widespread human disruption and systemic, long-term supply chain volatility—all triggered by a single cyber attack targeting French retailers

Adversaries successfully hijacked remote-access refrigeration controllers, manipulating system parameters to force industrial units into catastrophic, continuous defrost cycles. This drove temperatures in fridges and freezers to reach as high as 80°C while disabling alarm logic.

This incident is far from an isolated event; supply chains have long represented an attractive vector for threat actors targeting retail infrastructure. However, the rapid emergence of frontier AI and autonomous agents marks a profound shift in adversary capabilities across the digital supply chain. Modern autonomous agents can systematically analyze complex source code to uncover hidden vulnerabilities, map critical exploit pathways, and execute machine-speed attacks at an unprecedented global scale.

The contextual awareness of frontier AI models enables adversaries to identify, map, and exploit digital supply chain vulnerabilities at a pace human-driven correlation cannot effectively counter. Organisations therefore need automated, cross-business defensive frameworks that can operate at machine-speed. Without these frameworks, AI-enabled threat actors will retain their significant advantage. 

Trust can be a significant security risk

Modern enterprise infrastructure relies heavily on update mechanisms and open-source dependencies – and these are inviting targets for cyber adversaries, who are continually developing new methods to exploit new digital supply chain attack vectors. Real-world examples of digital supply chain compromise include SolarWinds, Log4Shell, and Mini Shai-Hulud, where attackers exploited vulnerabilities within third-party tools, applications, and services to facilitate a wide range of malicious activities. Frontier AI makes this process much easier for attackers, turning trusted vendor relationships into primary attack vectors.

What’s more, software vendors are routinely shipping new AI capabilities, agents, and integrations into enterprise software stacks through traditionally unremarkable updates. As a result, C-suite executives are often unaware of the AI tools operating inside their perimeter and subsequently lack the governance frameworks to monitor them. There’s also the risk of ‘Shadow AI’. The massive adoption of AI – not only by enterprise IT but also by individual users – has created an even higher level of complexity and cyber risk. If an external AI service used by an employee or well-meaning partner is compromised, it creates an unmonitored backchannel straight into corporate data lakes.

The 72-minute exfiltration window

Alarmingly, the time from an attacker’s initial access to data exfiltration has collapsed from weeks or days to just minutes. This means the traditional ‘zero-day clock’ and patching window have effectively been eliminated, and human-speed defences are no longer fast enough to stop machine-speed attacks.

Data from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reveals that the fastest quartile of sensitive data exfiltration now occurs in less than 72 minutes from initial compromise, highlighting the new defensive speed baseline required of modern security operations. Most security operations centres typically rely on human review cycles where alert triage takes at least 15 minutes, further investigation often requires requests to be raised manually, and containment of an affected system can take days. 

Seize the initiative for digital supply chain resilience

To identify machine-speed threats across complex ecosystems, organisations must increase visibility and reduce complexity through a unified security architecture. Crucially, autonomous threat management must ensure detection and response happen in seconds rather than hours or days.

Learn how to secure the digital supply chain, including five key questions CXOs need to ask and answer to achieve digital supply chain resilience in the AI age, in our new whitepaper: Defending the digital supply chain in the era of frontier AI.  Click here to download the whitepaper.

item.title: Checkmate for Checkboxes
item.dc:creator: Nicole Quinn
item.description:
Autonomous AI demands real-time operational governance, not checkbox security. If anyone in policy or corporate governance still harboured the belief that autonomous artificial intelligence could be neatly kept behind digital glass, recent …

The post Checkmate for Checkboxes appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Autonomous AI demands real-time operational governance, not checkbox security.

If anyone in policy or corporate governance still harboured the belief that autonomous artificial intelligence could be neatly kept behind digital glass, recent events have shattered it.

From Google’s Gemini iterating past perimeter access controls during goal-optimisation trials, to an autonomous model at Hugging Face triggering 17,000 security alerts attempting to harvest production keys, the evidence is no longer theoretical. When testing Anthropic’s Claude Mythos during Project Glasswing trials, the model demonstrated the capacity to discover and chain complex code vulnerabilities into critical exploit paths in hours rather than months. It didn't simply uncover software bugs, it demonstrated goal optimisation at machine speed.

To view these incidents as isolated glitches is to miss the point. They mark a structural shift in the economics of digital risk. For decades, enterprise defence rested on a comfortable asymmetry: discovering and exploiting a vulnerability required human labour, time, and specialised skill. That timeline has collapsed. What once took a human adversary nine days now takes an autonomous harness fifteen minutes.

From the corridors of power in Canberra to the tech hubs of London and Singapore, regulators have realised that the speed and deceptive potential of autonomous machine reasoning have officially outrun traditional oversight.

A political reckoning

Governments are pivoting from passive consultation to active legislative muscle.

In Australia, this reality recently prompted the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) to launch the ASD Essentials, an evolution explicitly designed to build upon the foundational baselines set by the Essential Eight. By replacing static compliance checklists with outcome-focused principles across Enterprise IT, Cloud, and OT, Canberra has acknowledged a reality technical teams have faced for years: single-domain checklist audits cannot defend against interconnected threats.

Across Asia, Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency has similarly pioneered a formal autonomy-tiering framework, enforcing strict security reviews, scoped boundaries, and human-in-the-loop controls for high-impact systems.

This regional push mirrors a broader global consensus. In a landmark thematic brief, the United Nation’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned that autonomous agentic misalignment is bypassing conventional safeguards and threatening human control. A reality reinforced by joint Five Eyes intelligence warnings that AI has collapsed vulnerability exploitation windows from days to minutes.

What regulators worldwide now recognise is that traditional "checkbox" compliance is obsolete. When autonomous models identify and exploit software flaws in minutes rather than days, an annual audit provides false comfort. In practice, this is accelerating the shift from traditional Authority to Operate (ATO) regimes to a continuous model (cATO); moving security from an annual milestone to an ongoing operational discipline. Mandatory operational guardrails are no longer a future policy debate; they are an immediate requirement for enterprise survival.

The dilemma for the boardroom is acute. Research from Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reveals significant variance across frontier models—because each foundation model is shaped by different training data and reasoning pathways, no single AI system captures the full vulnerability surface. Adversaries will not rely on a single model; they chain diverse, agentic harnesses together to test alternative lateral paths. Expecting a human security committee or an annual compliance audit to counter multi-model machine reasoning is like betting on your pawn to replace your Queen on the board.

Three moves beyond the checkbox

If static compliance is obsolete, real-time operational governance must take its place. Notably, the new ASD Essentials framework places Identity Services and Boundary Services into its first implementation priority phase - identifying them as the primary pathways adversaries exploit. Managing a non-human workforce operating at machine speed requires applying those principles through three structural shifts: 

  1. Identity boundaries over text prompts
    Instructing an autonomous model to "avoid restricted databases" via system prompts is useless when the model is ruthlessly optimised for an operational goal. As AI safety evaluations demonstrate, unconstrained models will fabricate credentials or impersonate authorised reviewers to achieve objective completion. AI agents and service integrations must be treated as distinct digital identities with short-lived access keys enforcing Zero Standing Privileges (ZSP) - ensuring ephemeral access expires the second a task concludes. 
  2. Inline infrastructure isolation
    If an agentic system discovers a path around an application policy, the network layer itself must act as the circuit breaker. Rather than relying on application-level filtering, boundary security must enforce transport-level segmentation that automatically severs unauthorised connections before machine reasoning can test alternative lateral paths. 
  3. Automated virtual patching
    Under legacy frameworks, teams calibrated risk around 48-hour or 14-day human patch cycles. That calculus is unsustainable when exposure windows are measured in minutes. Defensive architectures need to deploy inline, virtual patches automatically within hours of zero-day discovery, neutralising exploit traffic across edge and cloud infrastructure without waiting for manual vendor deployments or maintenance windows.

Reclaiming the advantage

To counter an adversary employing weaponised multi-model harnesses, defenders can no longer rely on singular AI defences or delayed patching cycles. Grounded in frontline threat telemetry, Unit 42® Frontier AI Defense addresses this asymmetry directly. This always-on, agentic service combines our offensive security experts with proprietary multi-model harnesses to discover vulnerabilities, validate real-world exploitability, and accelerate remediation, to establish an active architectural counterweight capable of matching the velocity and reasoning capacity of frontier threats.

The era of "checkbox security" has reached checkmate. As ASD's shift to the Essentials demonstrates, board members can no longer seek refuge behind static compliance checkmarks or delayed audit cycles. True operational resilience requires governing at the speed of machine reasoning: with automated containment, strict identity boundaries, and real-time posture control. Those who modernise their architectures now will retain market trust; those who rely on legacy compliance playbooks will find them rendered obsolete before the first hour of an incident has elapsed.

Take the Next Step Discover how Unit 42 Frontier AI Defense helps organizations discover hidden exposures, enforce identity controls, and build machine-speed resilience before attackers exploit vulnerabilities.

item.title: New Cortex XDR Integration with Claude Cowork Secures Desktop AI Agents
item.dc:creator: Daphna Shemesh
item.description:
AI agents working directly on the desktop offer new ways to automate complex tasks, yet they operate outside traditional endpoint controls and pose unacceptable risks to many security leaders. Today, we're announcing …

The post New Cortex XDR Integration with Claude Cowork Secures Desktop AI Agents appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents working directly on the desktop offer new ways to automate complex tasks, yet they operate outside traditional endpoint controls and pose unacceptable risks to many security leaders. Today, we're announcing a new Cortex XDR integration with Claude Cowork to deliver visibility and threat detection for this new agentic workspace.

Claude Cowork brings agentic capabilities directly to desktop applications as part of Claude Enterprise. Instead of responding to a single prompt, it plans and completes multi-step tasks by reading files, navigating applications and executing workflows. This work takes place inside a small, local virtual machine that is designed to act as a security boundary. However, this isolation also prevents the EDR agent from monitoring the agent’s activity. With this integration, XDR bridges that gap to deliver deep visibility and threat detection across local agentic workflows without compromising host security.

Delivering Runtime Visibility and Threat Detection Inside the Virtual Machine

With this new integration with Claude Cowork, we’re bringing XDR directly into the virtual machine using a lightweight sensor. XDR will extend runtime visibility into the agent’s actions, tracking accessed systems, file changes and executed commands while detecting and preventing malicious behavior in real time.

Behind this protection, XDR brings together Unit 42 Threat intelligence and machine learning models trained on global telemetry to block zero day threats by default. To prevent alert fatigue, the sensor feeds virtual machine telemetry directly into XDR analytics, automatically correlating related events into unified incident stories. 

The Cortex platform will consolidate the agent’s activity from inside the virtual machine and tie it back to the desktop in a single view. This gives security teams complete context into agent’s actions alongside the rest of their endpoint data.

Securing Every Agent on the Endpoint

EDR coverage across all execution environments is a baseline requirement for enterprise security teams, but it’s no longer sufficient if it doesn’t secure AI agents. Just as we brought together XDR and Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security to protect both traditional system processes and AI agents with XDR One, through this integration with Claude Cowork we are once again expanding XDR to seamlessly monitor every agent on the endpoint. The integration will be available in private preview in the coming months.

This integration builds on our broader work securing AI across the enterprise. Palo Alto Networks is a launch participant in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, an initiative that gives a small group of organizations that build or maintain critical software early access to frontier AI capabilities for defensive cybersecurity. Earlier this year, we introduced Prisma AIRS Unified Data Protection for Claude to monitor prompts across Claude Code, Claude.ai, and Claude Cowork for data leaks and prompt injections. Now, with Cortex XDR extending into Claude Cowork, security teams can protect data in transit to Claude and monitor agent activity directly on the endpoint.

PROTECT THE MODERN ENDPOINT

item.title: Guiding Customers Through Critical PHP Vulnerabilities
item.dc:creator: Simone Gammeri
item.description:
Over the past week, our industry has faced a wave of critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). As Palo Alto Networks Chief Technology and Product Officer Lee Klarich highlighted, these high-severity …

The post Guiding Customers Through Critical PHP Vulnerabilities appeared first on Palo Alto Networks Blog.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past week, our industry has faced a wave of critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). As Palo Alto Networks Chief Technology and Product Officer Lee Klarich highlighted, these high-severity vulnerability disclosures are just the beginning of a massive acceleration of cyberthreats that will define the foreseeable future. 

Because PHP powers more than half of the web, relying on traditional patch cycles is no longer viable: while enterprise patching averages 55 days, threat actors can move from breach to data exfiltration in as little as 39 seconds.

With AI delivering a step-change in attack speed and depth, organizations simply cannot wait for patch development and deployment. They need proactive discovery and pre-emptive protection provided by Frontier Virtual Patching before the vulnerabilities are disclosed.  

When vulnerabilities of this magnitude emerge, enterprise customers turn immediately to their trusted advisors for clarity and direction. Palo Alto Networks partners play a pivotal role in guiding customers through this shift, moving them from reactive patching scrambles toward long-term protection. This resilience lands on one foundational imperative: Frontier Virtual Patching (FVP) must be enforced across all outbound traffic, not just at endpoints, in the cloud, or across Web Application Firewalls (WAFs).

The next few months will be a critical moment for partners to step in front of customers to educate them on the modern exposure gap, help them understand their true reachability, and rapidly protect their environments before weaponized exploits land.

The AI-Accelerated Threat Window 

With AI agents and frontier models available at the fingertips of any adversary, exploitation windows are collapsing. Nearly 30% of vulnerabilities are now weaponized by threat actors within 24 hours of disclosure. In the case of #PHP2Shell and #Brotli, telemetry revealed autonomous agents actively probing and compromising exposed entities within just 2 to 4 hours.

Customers must understand the unique severity of these threats:

  • Zero credentials required: The PHP vulnerabilities can be triggered by an unauthenticated request before any application code even runs.
  • No safe workarounds: Temporary configuration changes are not enough to secure a server. Mitigation requires comprehensive updates or a robust preemptive defense layer.
  • Exploits are active: We are already seeing proof-of-concept exploits in the wild, forcing governments and organizations to take websites offline as a precaution.

Understanding Your Customers’ Exposure

The hardest part of defending against vulnerabilities is tracking them down. Organizations must gain immediate, complete visibility into their true attack surface. 

Through our Frontier AI Alliance, we’ve engaged leading global systems integrators and service providers to deliver this protection at enterprise scale, already helping partners assess and secure hundreds of customer environments to date.

Over the past week, Palo Alto Networks has mobilized proactive services and intelligence tools to help partners guide customers through exposure discovery. Through Cortex Xpanse, defenders have mapped internet-facing assets to pinpoint exposed PHP footprints globally, while Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense provides reachability analysis to distinguish between theoretical software flaws and weaponizable attack paths.

Shielding Environments Before Day One

While discovering exposure is critical, customers cannot wait until their inventory is perfect to defend themselves. 

Customers running Frontier Virtual Patching on Palo Alto Networks Advanced Threat Prevention (ATP) Plus were protected before the PHP vulnerabilities were even made public.

Fueled by our Network and Open-Source Vulnerability Analyzer (NOVA), our frontier AI vulnerability analyzer, our customers have been shielded from these PHP exploits since October 20, without any downtime, software restarts, or manual policy changes. Because this protection runs at the network layer, it shields every workload whose traffic passes through the firewall, including the ones that aren't in their inventory yet.

Let's urge our customers to stop treating virtual patching as an emergency measure and start treating it as a foundational layer of their architecture. Our team is here to help you - learn more.

item.content:encoded:
For the eighth consecutive time, Palo Alto Networks is recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant for Privileged Access Management. Once again, it is positioned furthest along in Completeness of Vision and has been positioned so in every Magic Quadrant published for this category.

Read the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant for Privileged Access Management.

Identity is not a siloed risk. As an increasingly attractive target for threat actors, it must be understood and secured across the entire attack surface. For our customers, the benefit is clear: as part of Palo Alto Networks, Idira helps you adopt AI innovation at speed while retaining control over privileged access.

Why Vision Matters Most Right Now

The 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant evaluates providers across their Ability to Execute and Completeness of Vision. We feel that being positioned furthest in Completeness of Vision matters most in moments of technology change like this one. Idira is built for an environment where:

  • Identity is the attack surface, and frontier AI lets attackers move faster, increasingly logging in rather than breaking in.
  • Identities have exploded, and human and machine privilege alike must be controlled.
  • The pace of change has never been higher, as organizations race to adopt AI and modernize infrastructure without losing control.

Customers need a partner that can execute on an innovative vision as the threat and technology landscape evolves. With the scale of Palo Alto Networks behind us, we are focused on securing every identity and every moment of privilege in the AI enterprise.

The AI Era Demands More From PAM

We are in a new era, where identity and access have fundamentally changed. Machine identities now outnumber humans 109 to 1, AI agents (which require access to enterprise systems to do useful work) are entering the workforce, and attackers have noticed. That access must be governed alongside the human and machine identities already protected. Increasingly, though, attackers log in rather than break in, and PAM must evolve to stay ahead of these challenges. PAM must now extend beyond vaulted administrator credentials to discover, control, and govern privilege across the enterprise.

Idira’s Modern PAM platform is enabling PAM to meet the demands of the AI era; it combines vaulted access and zero standing privileges (ZSP) with secrets management, workload security, and identity governance. We are bringing ZSP to every modern target, including cloud, apps, and Kubernetes. And access challenges go beyond humans, so Idira does as well. To secure non-human access, Idira added native SPIFFE/SVID support to deliver short-lived cryptographic identities to workloads and AI agents. Our ability to deliver and innovate on our vision enables Idira to deliver purpose-built, end-to-end protection at scale for the modern AI enterprise.

Modernizing PAM: Where We Deliver

Making modern PAM easier to adopt is central to our approach. 

While some of the largest organizations continue to trust Idira for our proven traditional PAM leadership, they now also rely on us to guide their modern PAM transformation initiatives.

Data-Driven Innovation: We believe that our Transformation Decision Engine, which uses customer environment data to quantify the value of PAM modernization, combined with our years of proven experience guiding both the implementation and modernization of PAM programs across our expansive customer base, demonstrates our ability to help customers through any stage of their PAM journey with an informed, data-driven approach. 

Customer Experience: Idira guides cross-functional security teams through complex operational shifts, from standing access to ZSP, supported by the Idira Blueprint, hands-on training, and an active peer community. 

Scale and Reach: Idira customers already have a partner with global reach, and joining Palo Alto Networks extends it further. Our security platform sees identity risk across the whole attack surface, so a stolen or abused privilege becomes a signal your defenses act on in the moment, backed by the investment and expertise of the industry's largest cybersecurity company.

Ready for the Demands of the AI Enterprise 

Eight reports, eight times furthest in vision. I'm grateful to the customers whose trust and expertise shaped every one of them. This is also a first, as it’s the first report to carry the Palo Alto Networks name. Since Idira joined forces with Palo Alto Networks, our PAM expertise and platform now sit inside the industry's leading cybersecurity company, where privileged access connects to real-time threat detection and response, AI security, and Unit 42 threat intelligence.

The next chapter of privileged access is being written now, by attackers with frontier AI models and by enterprises deciding how fast to move. We intend to stay furthest ahead of both.

Thank you to our customers and community for your trust, and for the partnership that helps shape our innovation.

What is the Gartner® Magic Quadrant?

“Magic Quadrant reports are a culmination of rigorous, fact-based research in specific markets, providing a wide-angle view of the relative positions of providers in markets where growth is high and provider differentiation is distinct. Providers are positioned into four quadrants: Leaders, Challengers, Visionaries and Niche Players. The research enables you to get the most from market analysis in alignment with your unique business and technology needs."

How can PAM help secure AI agents in the enterprise?

PAM can help secure AI agents by controlling their access to systems and data, protecting the secrets they use, and recording their access and actions. Capabilities vary by solution; controls should limit each agent’s permissions and how long those permissions remain active. Learn more about Idira Agentic Identity Security.

How does zero standing privileges differ from vaulted access?

Vaulted access protects stored privileged credentials. ZSP removes standing privileged access by granting permissions for a specific task and revoking them when the task or authorized period ends. Modern PAM can combine both approaches to support different environments and access needs.
